clue.text: One dumb spy novel? Not book for Le Carré, maybe

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new or fresh, so these letters are made into a new arrangement
Not tells us to leave something out of the letters before they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A reviewer sneers at a silly spy thriller, saying it hardly deserves the name book, and wonders about John le Carré.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing B from ONEDUMBSPY leaves ONEDUMSPY, which 'novel' rearranges. 'spy novel' looks like a phrase, but 'novel' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: John le Carré was the pen name of David Cornwell, so he is an example of a writer using an assumed name.

clue.text: Like some kids' books from Jerry Springer when young?

parts.note: jerry is British slang for a chamber pot, which crosswords shorten to po
a springer spaniel when young is a puppy, a pup

explanation.surface: Asks whether the TV host Jerry Springer, as a child, owned books whose pictures stand up off the page.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerry Springer looks like the talk-show host; split him into a chamber pot (jerry) and a dog breed (springer spaniel).
explanation.definitionFit: Pop-up books have cardboard scenes that rise up when the pages are opened, a common format for children.

clue.text: Specialist's keeping me in, when ill, for tests

indicators.note: keeping means holding something within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: specialist's is read as specialist is, a specialist being an expert, giving experts

indicators.note: ill means badly, so the letters are put into a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: A medical specialist keeps a patient in hospital for tests while they are unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when ill' rearranges ME IN into IMEN. The apostrophe in 'Specialist's' is read as 'is', so the specialist piece is plural-looking but singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Experiments are trials carried out to discover or confirm something, so they are tests.

clue.text: Felt irritation following daughter getting dumped

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the irritation piece is placed after the daughter piece

parts.note: D is the usual abbreviation for daughter, as in family trees
to have felt irritation on the skin is to have itched

explanation.surface: Someone felt irritated after their daughter was abandoned by a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to abandon or discard it, so ditched is a synonym of dumped.

clue.text: Snooping has one boy up before head

indicators.note: before means the reversed piece comes ahead of the next piece
in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a boy is a son
a ness is a headland, a head of land jutting into the sea, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Inverness

explanation.surface: Someone has a boy who stays up before the headmaster, caught prying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses I SON to make NOSI. NESS is a headland, as in Orford Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosiness is being overly curious about other people's affairs, which is what snooping amounts to.

clue.text: Animal disease besets European riding school

indicators.note: besets means surrounds or hems in, so the disease word goes around the other piece

parts.note: a skin complaint of dogs and other animals caused by mites

explanation.surface: A disease among the animals plagues a European riding school.
explanation.definitionFit: A manège is a school or enclosed arena where horses and riders are trained, a borrowing from French.

clue.text: Bust, or the opposite of bust around start of season

indicators.note: around means the boom piece wraps round the next piece

parts.note: in economics, boom and bust are opposites

indicators.note: start of picks the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether a business enjoyed a boom or a collapse at the start of the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' appears twice: first as the definition (chest), then in the economic sense, whose opposite is BOOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a woman's chest, and bosom is a synonym for that part of the body.

clue.text: Perch can be swimming round a lake

indicators.note: round means the anagrammed letters go round the other pieces
swimming suggests letters moving about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A perch, the fish, may be found swimming around a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' rearranges CAN BE into BANCE, which goes round A and L. 'Perch' looks like the fish; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To perch is to sit or stand precariously on something, which is to balance.

clue.text: Lay some false trails

indicators.note: some means only part of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Someone lays down misleading trails for pursuers.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something down is to set it, as in laying or setting a table or a trap.

clue.text: Star with money playing Glastonbury?

indicators.note: playing, like an instrument played freely, signals the letters being rearranged

explanation.surface: A big-name star is paid a fortune to play the Glastonbury music festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Glastonbury looks like the music festival, but it is the medieval abbey in Somerset, England; the question mark marks this as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Glastonbury Abbey was a great Benedictine religious house, so it is an example of a home for monks.

clue.text: Singer, one with piano in place of orchestra

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
one is the Roman numeral I
the orchestra pit is where the band plays in a theatre

explanation.surface: A singer works with a pianist in the space where the orchestra would normally be.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipit is a small songbird, and crosswords often call birds singers.

clue.text: The only one in a suit wearing vest?

definitions.text: The only one in a suit

parts.note: in British usage a vest is an undershirt, also called a singlet
wearing something is having it on

explanation.surface: Pictures the only man in a formal suit, wondering whether he has a vest on underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' looks like clothing, matching the vest, but it is a suit of cards: in bridge a singleton is a lone card in a suit.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games a singleton is a hand's sole card of a particular suit.

clue.text: Reproduction of Stonehenge repositioned in capital

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters are placed inside the capital city

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France

indicators.note: repositioned means the stones, the letters, are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Imagines a replica of Stonehenge being moved and rebuilt in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repositioned' rearranges the monument's name into THENOGENES. 'Reproduction' looks like a copy of the monument, but it is biological.
explanation.definitionFit: Parthenogenesis is reproduction from an unfertilised egg, without a male, a type of breeding.

clue.text: Important instruction to proxy about ratifying document?

definitions.text: instruction to proxy about ratifying document?
definitions.meaning: split up, the answer reads as a note telling a stand-in to put a signature on a document in your absence

explanation.surface: Someone stresses a key message to a stand-in about signing a document.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is read as the phrase 'sign if I can't', an instruction left for a proxy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something significant carries real weight or meaning, so it is important.

clue.text: How Mussorgsky introduced himself, being vain?

definitions.meaning: the composer's first name was Modest, so he would have greeted people with 'I am Modest'
vain means conceited, boastful about oneself

explanation.walkthrough: The Russian composer Modest Mussorgsky's first name makes his self-introduction ironically claim humility, the opposite of the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An immodest person shows off and thinks too highly of themselves, which is being vain.

clue.text: Conservative coming in for new, original abuse

indicators.note: coming in for means taking the place of, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: an original idea is an inventive one
C is the abbreviation for Conservative, the British political party

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician arrives to replace a new member, prompting fresh insults.
explanation.walkthrough: In INVENTIVE, the second N becomes C.
explanation.definitionFit: Invective is abusive, insulting language, so it means verbal abuse.

clue.text: Harrier is British bird

parts.note: an eagle is a bird of prey

explanation.surface: States that the Harrier, a hawk, is a British bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A harrier looks like a bird of prey, matching 'bird', but here it is a hunting dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A harrier is a hound used to hunt hares; the beagle is a smaller hound of the same type.

clue.text: Rum is sweet stuff

definitions.meaning: a dark rum made in Guyana is named after the ... region
a brown cane sugar is named after the same region

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the adjective meaning odd, but it is the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara names both a Guyanese rum and a crunchy brown sugar from the same region.

clue.text: Japan, say, wants river to evaporate

indicators.note: wants here means lacks, so a letter is missing

parts.note: japan is a hard glossy lacquer, a kind of varnish

explanation.surface: A country such as Japan wants a river to dry up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Japan' looks like the country but is a lacquer, an example of varnish, hence 'say'. 'wants' removes R.
explanation.definitionFit: To evaporate is to disappear into vapour, so to vanish.

clue.text: It's about basic education disrupted by English troublemaker

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: the letters of the word as written, without the apostrophe

indicators.note: disrupted by means another piece breaks into the middle of this one

parts.note: the three Rs, reading, writing and arithmetic, are the basics of education

explanation.surface: A troublemaker in class disrupts basic lessons in English.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs (reading, writing, arithmetic) are the basics of schooling; 'disrupted by' puts E among them, making RRER, and 'about' turns the clue's ITS round.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrer is someone who deliberately stirs up trouble, a troublemaker.

clue.text: Score equally split between Liverpool and Sunderland? That shows doggedness

definitions.text: Score equally split between Liverpool and Sunderland?
definitions.meaning: twenty shared equally between two cities gives ten per city

explanation.walkthrough: 'a' means 'per', so twenty divided between two cities is 'ten a city'. Liverpool and Sunderland are English cities, and 'Score' suggests football.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenacity is the quality of holding on firmly and not giving up, which is doggedness.

clue.text: Praise a double century, first for Moeen Ali possibly

indicators.note: double means the letter for a century is written twice

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters may be arranged in another order
first for picks the initial letter of the following name

explanation.surface: Moeen Ali, the England cricketer, might win praise for scoring a double century for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges M (from Moeen) and ALI into LAIM. A century in cricket is a hundred runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public approval, a synonym of praise.

clue.text: Lump party together with voting upset

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: A political party is lumped together with a disastrous vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses POLL into LLOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollop is a shapeless mass of something soft, like a lump of mashed potato.

clue.text: His nice shop can supply haggis finally? Buy it!

indicators.note: supply is read as supplely, in a flexible way, so the letters bend into a new order
finally picks the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: An advert for a Scottish shop that can supply haggis, ending with 'Buy it!'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' rearranges HIS NICE SHOP CAN; the S from haggis goes on the end. 'Buy it' looks like a shopping slogan; it is slang for die.
explanation.definitionFit: To buy it is slang for dying, and cashing in one's chips is an idiom for dying too.

clue.text: Surrounded by most of family, I resigned

indicators.note: surrounded by means the letter is placed inside the other piece
most of means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: stock means family line or ancestry

explanation.surface: Surrounded by most of the family, someone gives up their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims STOCK to STOC, and 'Surrounded by' puts I inside it. 'resigned' looks like quitting a job; it means accepting things.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoic person accepts hardship calmly without complaint, which is to be resigned.

clue.text: Lay to rest a recurrent worry, among other things

parts.note: to inter is to bury, to lay to rest

indicators.note: recurrent is read as running back, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: ail means to trouble or worry someone

explanation.surface: Putting a nagging, returning anxiety to rest, among other matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurrent' reverses AIL into LIA. 'Lay to rest a recurrent worry' reads as one phrase about settling an anxiety.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter alia is a Latin phrase meaning among other things.

clue.text: Stomach-turning jerk

indicators.note: turning means turned round, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: the gut is the stomach

explanation.surface: A nauseating, revolting idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach-turning' looks like 'disgusting', and 'jerk' like an insult; 'turning' reverses GUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tug is a sudden hard pull, a jerk.

clue.text: Mission accomplished, leave and move on, first of all

indicators.note: first of all means taking the opening letter of every one of the words

explanation.surface: A job done, an agent is told to leave and move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mission accomplished' looks like a single phrase; 'Mission' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo in Texas was a Spanish mission, a religious outpost, before its famous siege in 1836.

clue.text: Rave about entertaining Latin composer

indicators.note: entertaining means holding as a guest, so one piece goes inside the other
about means turned round, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: to rave is to rage, to rant furiously

explanation.surface: A rave review praises a composer for his entertaining Latin music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses RAGE into EGAR, and 'entertaining' puts L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward Elgar was an English composer, known for the Enigma Variations.

clue.text: Hard-headed idiot in charge holds yearly meeting

indicators.note: holds means contains, so the meeting goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: prat is British slang for a fool
AGM is the annual general meeting

explanation.surface: A foolish chairman runs the annual meeting, though he claims to be practical.
explanation.definitionFit: A pragmatic person is practical and realistic, not sentimental, which is being hard-headed.
